section.title: The Priestly Garments
section.sectionRationale: With the structure of the tabernacle described, God now turns to the men who will minister in it: Aaron and his sons are set apart to serve as priests, and their garments, ephod, breastpiece, robe, and turban, are designed for glory and splendor, marking them as mediators who carry Israel before the LORD.
section.thesis: God commands holy garments for Aaron and his sons so that they may serve as priests, carrying the names of Israel's tribes over their hearts and shoulders and bearing the inscription Holy to the LORD on their foreheads.
section.frameNote: Five movements: Aaron and his sons set apart for the priesthood; the ephod bearing the memorial stones; the breastpiece of judgment with the Urim and Thummim; the robe with its bells and pomegranates; and the gold plate, turban, and remaining garments.

units.label: Aaron set apart to serve as priest

media.alt: A priest robed in blue, gold, and white
media.caption: Aaron and his sons are clothed in holy garments to serve the LORD as priests.

verses.text: “Next, have your brother Aaron brought to you from among the Israelites, along with his sons Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar, to serve Me as priests.
Make holy garments for your brother Aaron, to give him glory and splendor.
You are to instruct all the skilled craftsmen, whom I have filled with a spirit of wisdom, to make garments for Aaron's consecration, so that he may serve Me as priest.

These are the garments that they shall make: a breastpiece, an ephod, a robe, a woven tunic, a turban, and a sash. They are to make these holy garments for your brother Aaron and his sons, so that they may serve Me as priests.
They shall use gold, along with blue, purple, and scarlet yarn, and fine linen.
They are to make the {{ephod|ephod}} of finely spun linen embroidered with gold, and with blue, purple, and scarlet yarn.
It shall have two shoulder pieces attached at two of its corners, so it can be fastened.
And the skillfully woven waistband of the ephod must be of one piece, of the same workmanship, with gold, with blue, purple, and scarlet yarn, and with finely spun linen.
Take two onyx stones and engrave on them the names of the sons of Israel:
six of their names on one stone and the remaining six on the other, in the order of their birth.
Engrave the names of the sons of Israel on the two stones the way a gem cutter engraves a seal. Then mount the stones in gold filigree settings.
Fasten both stones on the shoulder pieces of the ephod as memorial stones for the sons of Israel. Aaron is to bear their names on his two shoulders as a memorial before the LORD.
Fashion gold filigree settings
and two chains of pure gold, made of braided cord work; and attach these chains to the settings.
You are also to make a {{breastpiece|breastpiece}} of judgment with the same workmanship as the ephod. Construct it with gold, with blue, purple, and scarlet yarn, and with finely spun linen.
It must be square when folded over double, a span long and a span wide.
And mount on it a setting of gemstones, four rows of stones: In the first row there shall be a ruby, a topaz, and an emerald;
in the second row a turquoise, a sapphire, and a diamond;
in the third row a jacinth, an agate, and an amethyst;
and in the fourth row a beryl, an onyx, and a jasper. Mount these stones in gold filigree settings.
The twelve stones are to correspond to the names of the sons of Israel, each engraved like a seal with the name of one of the twelve tribes.
For the breastpiece, make braided chains like cords of pure gold.
You are also to make two gold rings and fasten them to the two corners of the breastpiece.
Then fasten the two gold chains to the two gold rings at the corners of the breastpiece,
and fasten the other ends of the two chains to the two filigree settings, attaching them to the shoulder pieces of the ephod at the front.
Make two more gold rings and attach them to the other two corners of the breastpiece, on the inside edge next to the ephod.
Make two additional gold rings and attach them to the bottom of the two shoulder pieces of the ephod, on its front, near its seam just above its woven waistband.
The rings of the breastpiece shall be tied to the rings of the ephod with a cord of blue yarn, so that the breastpiece is above the waistband of the ephod and does not swing out from the ephod.
Whenever Aaron enters the Holy Place, he shall bear the names of the sons of Israel over his heart on the breastpiece of judgment, as a continual reminder before the LORD.

And place the {{urim|Urim and Thummim}} in the breastpiece of judgment, so that they will also be over Aaron's heart whenever he comes before the LORD. Aaron will continually carry the judgment of the sons of Israel over his heart before the LORD.

units.label: The robe, bells, and pomegranates
units.note: so that he will not die

verses.text: You are to make the robe of the ephod entirely of blue cloth,
with an opening at its top in the center. Around the opening shall be a woven collar with an opening like that of a garment, so that it will not tear.
Make pomegranates of blue, purple, and scarlet yarn all the way around the lower hem, with gold bells between them,
alternating the gold bells and pomegranates around the lower hem of the robe.
Aaron must wear the robe whenever he ministers, and its sound will be heard when he enters or exits the sanctuary before the LORD, so that he will not die.

units.label: Holy to the LORD
units.note: the gold plate, turban, and remaining garments

verses.text: You are to make a plate of pure gold and engrave on it as on a seal: {{holy|HOLY TO THE LORD}}.
Fasten to it a blue cord to mount it on the turban; it shall be on the front of the turban.

And it will be worn on Aaron's forehead, so that he may bear the iniquity of the holy things that the sons of Israel consecrate with regard to all their holy gifts. It shall always be on his forehead, so that they may be acceptable before the LORD.
You are to weave the tunic with fine linen, make the turban of fine linen, and fashion an embroidered sash.
Make tunics, sashes, and headbands for Aaron's sons, to give them glory and splendor.
After you put these garments on your brother Aaron and his sons, anoint them, ordain them, and consecrate them so that they may serve Me as priests.
Make linen undergarments to cover their bare flesh, extending from waist to thigh.

Aaron and his sons must wear them whenever they enter the Tent of Meeting or approach the altar to minister in the Holy Place, so that they will not incur guilt and die. This is to be a permanent statute for Aaron and his descendants.

ephod.gloss: A richly woven, apron-like garment worn over the robe, joined at the shoulders and fastened with a waistband. It held the memorial stones bearing Israel's tribal names and anchored the breastpiece to the high priest's body.

breastpiece.gloss: The breastpiece of judgment, a jeweled pouch worn over the heart holding twelve gemstones engraved with the tribal names, and containing the Urim and Thummim used to discern God's will in judgment.

urim.gloss: Urim and Thummim, likely meaning lights and perfections, objects placed in the breastpiece used to discern God's decisions in matters of judgment. Their exact nature is not described, but they functioned as a means of seeking God's verdict.

holy.gloss: Holy to the LORD, an inscription on the gold plate worn on Aaron's forehead. It declared Aaron, and through him the whole nation's worship, set apart exclusively for God, even as he bore the guilt of Israel's imperfect offerings.

basic.context: God now describes the garments Aaron and his sons must wear to serve as priests: an ephod bearing Israel's tribes on the shoulders, a breastpiece bearing them over the heart, a robe with bells so Aaron would not die entering God's presence, and a gold plate reading Holy to the LORD on his forehead.
basic.hermeneutics: These are literal vestments for Israel's actual priesthood under the old covenant, designed with real functions, memorial, mediation, discernment, and holiness, not merely decorative religious costume. Their meaning is drawn out directly by the text itself: memorial stones, a breastpiece of judgment, an inscription of holiness.
basic.originalLanguages: The ephod and choshen, breastpiece, together carried Israel's twelve tribes literally on Aaron's shoulders and over his heart whenever he entered the Holy Place. The urim vetummim within the breastpiece served to discern God's judgment, while the plate reading qodesh la-Yahweh, holy to the LORD, marked Aaron himself as consecrated wholly to God.
basic.typology: Aaron carrying Israel's names on his shoulders and over his heart pictures a mediator who represents the people bodily before God, fulfilled in Christ, who bears His people always before the Father. The plate reading Holy to the LORD anticipates Christ's perfect holiness, which makes even imperfect worship acceptable to God.
basic.christ: Hebrews presents Jesus as the great high priest who always lives to intercede for His people, Hebrews 7:25, carrying them before God far more perfectly than Aaron's engraved stones ever could. Where Aaron bore the guilt of Israel's holy things so they would be accepted, Christ bears His people's sin fully so that they are made acceptable once for all.
basic.god: God cares intensely about how His priests approach Him, prescribing exact garments down to bells on a hem, showing both the seriousness of mediating for a holy God and His gracious provision of a way for that mediation to succeed rather than end in death.
basic.crossReferences: Hebrews 4:14-16 presents Jesus as the great high priest through whom believers approach God's throne with confidence. Hebrews 7:25 says He always lives to intercede for those who come to God through Him. 1 Peter 2:9 calls the whole church a holy priesthood.
basic.oneStory: Aaron was clothed to carry Israel's names before God, bearing their guilt so their worship would be accepted, on pain of death if he entered carelessly. Christ is the true and greater High Priest who carries His people fully and perfectly before the Father, making every believer who trusts Him permanently acceptable before God.

context.literary:
Exodus 25 to 31 is one long address from God to Moses on the mountain, marked off into seven speeches by the formula 'the LORD said to Moses,' Exodus 25:1, 30:11, 30:17, 30:22, 30:34, 31:1 and 31:12. Chapter 28 belongs to the first and longest of them. Chapters 25 to 27 worked from the ark outward to the courtyard; now the plan turns from the house to the man who will serve in it.

The chapter describes the garments from the outside in and from the most glorious to the most humble: ephod, verses 6 to 14; breastpiece, verses 15 to 30; robe, verses 31 to 35; gold plate and turban, verses 36 to 38; then the tunics, sashes, headbands and undergarments, verses 39 to 43. When Aaron is actually dressed the order runs the other way, from the skin outward: tunic, sash, robe, ephod, breastpiece, turban and plate, Exodus 29:5-6 and Leviticus 8:7-9. The plan is written to be seen; the dressing is written to be done.

Two phrases bind the chapter together. The first is an inclusio: the garments are 'to give him glory and splendor,' verse 2, and the sons' plainer garments are 'to give them glory and splendor,' verse 40. The second is the verb 'bear.' Aaron bears the names on his shoulders, verse 12, bears them over his heart, verse 29, bears the judgment of Israel, verse 30, and bears the iniquity of the holy things, verse 38. Verse 43 turns the same idea into a warning: priests who approach wrongly 'incur guilt and die,' literally bear iniquity themselves. Alongside it runs 'before the LORD,' six times between verses 12 and 38, and the word 'continual,' verses 29, 30 and 38. Everything Aaron wears faces God.

Within the book the chapter sets up a painful irony. Four chapters later the man for whom gold filigree and engraved stones were designed takes Israel's gold earrings and fashions a calf with an engraving tool, Exodus 32:2-4.
context.historical:
These instructions were given at Sinai, and the garments were made after the golden calf crisis, when the people's offerings finally arrived, Exodus 39:1-31. Moses then dressed Aaron in them at the ordination recorded in Leviticus 8:7-9.

The materials are the materials of the sanctuary itself. The curtains of the tabernacle and the veil before the Most Holy Place were woven of finely spun linen with blue, purple and scarlet yarn, Exodus 26:1 and 26:31, and the ephod and breastpiece use the same mix with gold worked in. The high priest was dressed in the fabric of the house of God. Blue and purple dyes were among the costliest goods of the ancient world and were associated with royalty, so the garments carried the look of a court as well as a shrine. Every Israelite also wore a thread of that colour: a blue cord on the tassels of their garments, given so that they would 'be holy to your God,' Numbers 15:38-40.

Engraving 'the way a gem cutter engraves a seal,' verses 11, 21 and 36, draws on a familiar practice. Seals marked ownership and authority, and a name cut into stone was meant to last. The BSB footnote to verse 17 rightly warns that some of the gemstones cannot be identified with certainty; ancient stone names do not map neatly onto modern ones.

The ephod appears later in more than one form. The boy Samuel and King David each wore a simple linen ephod, 1 Samuel 2:18 and 2 Samuel 6:14. David asked for the priestly ephod when he needed guidance, 1 Samuel 23:9, and the Urim were consulted for Joshua, Numbers 27:21. Gideon's private ephod, by contrast, became an object of worship, Judges 8:27. After the exile no priest could consult the Urim and Thummim, Ezra 2:63, which suggests the objects were lost with the first temple. The garments themselves passed from father to son, as when Moses stripped Aaron on Mount Hor and dressed Eleazar, Numbers 20:26-28.
context.canonical:
The chapter is carried out almost word for word in Exodus 39, where each garment ends with the refrain 'just as the LORD had commanded Moses,' and it is put into practice at Aaron's ordination, Leviticus 8:7-9. Leviticus 16:4 adds a striking contrast: on the Day of Atonement the high priest lays aside the gold and colour and enters the Most Holy Place in plain linen. Psalm 133:2 remembers the anointing oil running down Aaron's beard 'over the collar of his robes,' the opening of verse 32.

The prophets reach for these garments when they speak of restoration. In Zechariah 3:3-5 the high priest Joshua stands in filthy clothes until the angel says, 'See, I have removed your iniquity,' and a clean turban is set on his head, the very place the gold plate belonged. Zechariah 14:20 then takes the inscription of verse 36 and spreads it across ordinary life: 'HOLY TO THE LORD will be inscribed on the bells of the horses.' Isaiah 61:10 pictures the redeemed clothed in garments of salvation 'as a bridegroom wears a priestly headdress.' Ezekiel 28:13 lists nine of the breastpiece stones among the adornments of one who was 'in Eden, the garden of God.'

The New Testament takes the office up directly. Hebrews 5:1-5 defines a high priest from Aaron's pattern, one called by God to represent people 'in matters relating to God,' and then shows Christ called by the Father. Hebrews 7:24-26 and 9:24 set Christ in heaven itself 'to appear on our behalf in the presence of God,' the true meaning of 'before the LORD.' John sees the risen Christ 'dressed in a long robe, with a golden sash around His chest,' Revelation 1:13. And the new Jerusalem gathers the chapter's jewels and names: gates 'inscribed with the names of the twelve tribes of Israel,' Revelation 21:12, foundations of precious stones, 21:19-20, and God's name on the foreheads of all His servants, 22:4.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Israel had just been told that they were to be 'a kingdom of priests and a holy nation,' Exodus 19:6, and in the same chapter they were warned not to touch the mountain or break through to see the LORD, Exodus 19:12 and 19:21. Moses writes this chapter into that tension. A whole people called to be near God cannot yet come near, so God appoints one man to stand in for them, and dresses him in a way that makes his meaning visible.

The first hearers were meant to see themselves on Aaron. Every tribe, the eldest and the youngest, was cut into stone 'in the order of their birth,' verse 10, and carried in on shoulders and heart. When Aaron entered the tent, Israel entered with him. They were also meant to grasp that the whole design came from God, not from Aaron's taste or rank; it was Moses who was to put the garments on him, verse 41, and craftsmen filled with 'a spirit of wisdom' who made them, verse 3.

Finally, the warnings 'so that he will not die,' verse 35, and 'so that they will not incur guilt and die,' verse 43, taught Israel that approaching the Holy One is never casual. The priest lives because he comes clothed as God has said. That lesson prepares for the atonement laws of Leviticus and for the grief of Leviticus 10:1-2, when two of the sons named in verse 1 died for offering what God had not commanded.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter is command, not narrative, but it commands one family for one covenant arrangement. It is 'a permanent statute for Aaron and his descendants,' verse 43, and Hebrews explains that 'when the priesthood is changed, the law must be changed as well,' Hebrews 7:12. The New Testament never assigns special robes to elders or ministers, so the chapter cannot be used as a warrant for clerical vestments, nor as a rule that worship must be ornate.

What carries forward are the realities the garments were made to show. God's people need a representative before Him, and they have one in Christ. Beauty offered to God is not vanity; the same God who demanded skill and splendour here values what is well made. Approaching God is done on His terms. And because the church is now 'a royal priesthood,' 1 Peter 2:9, every believer shares something of Aaron's work, carrying others before God in 'petitions, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgiving,' 1 Timothy 2:1.

debates.question: What were the Urim and Thummim, and how did they give an answer?

views.label: Sacred lots with a limited set of answers
views.case: In 1 Samuel 14:41 Saul asks God to 'respond with Urim' if the fault is with himself or Jonathan and 'with Thummim' if it lies with the people, and the choice falls one way. That reads like a lot giving one of two outcomes. 1 Samuel 28:6 adds that sometimes God 'did not answer,' which suggests a third result was possible. On this view the objects were two stones or tokens kept in the folded pouch of the breastpiece, verse 16.

views.label: A means of revelation tied to the breastpiece stones
views.case: Some later Jewish tradition connected the Urim with the gemstones of the breastpiece, as though the stones themselves signalled God's answer. The names, 'Lights and Perfections' in the BSB footnote, suited that idea. Scripture never describes such a mechanism, however, and verse 30 places the Urim and Thummim in the breastpiece as something added to it, not as the stones already mounted on it.

views.label: Deliberately undescribed
views.case: Others stress that the text, having described the garments down to rings and cords, says nothing about what the Urim and Thummim looked like. The silence may be the point: the answer came from God, not from a technique the priest could master. They disappear after the monarchy, and Ezra 2:63 waits for a priest who could use them again.

debates.bearing: Whatever their form, verse 30 calls them 'the judgment of the sons of Israel' carried over Aaron's heart. God's guidance for His people was bound up with the priest who loved and represented them, and it was God, not the object, who decided.

debates.question: What does it mean that Aaron will 'bear the iniquity of the holy things,' verse 38?

views.label: He carries the guilt as a substitute
views.case: The phrase is the one used of the scapegoat, which 'will carry on itself all their iniquities,' Leviticus 16:22, and of the Servant, who 'bore the sin of many,' Isaiah 53:12. Even Israel's offerings were stained by imperfection, and the high priest takes that stain upon himself so that the gifts 'may be acceptable before the LORD.'

views.label: He secures the lifting away of guilt
views.case: The same verb with the same noun can mean to forgive, as in Exodus 34:7, 'forgiving iniquity, transgression, and sin.' Read that way, the plate announces that God removes the defects of the people's worship, and Aaron is the appointed means by which that removal happens.

views.label: He answers for the sanctuary
views.case: Numbers 18:1 tells Aaron and his sons that they 'must bear the iniquity involving the sanctuary,' meaning they are held accountable for its proper use. On this view verse 38 describes the high priest's responsibility for everything Israel brings to God.

debates.bearing: The readings overlap more than they compete. Aaron is accountable, his office secures acceptance, and it does so by his carrying what is not his own. The New Testament gathers all three into Christ, who bore sin and now lives to intercede.

debates.question: Does John's seamless tunic, John 19:23-24, allude to the high priest's robe?

views.label: A deliberate priestly echo
views.case: The robe of the ephod was woven with a collar 'so that it will not tear,' verse 32, and the high priest was forbidden to tear his garments, Leviticus 21:10. John alone notes that Jesus' tunic was 'woven in one piece' and that the soldiers said, 'Let us not tear it.' Some interpreters have heard a hint that the one dying was the true high priest, while the high priest in the trial tore his clothes, Matthew 26:65.

views.label: A detail explained by Psalm 22
views.case: Others note that John states his own reason for recording the detail. John 19:24 quotes Psalm 22:18: 'They divided My garments among them, and cast lots for My clothing.' The word John uses is the ordinary word for a tunic, not the robe of verse 31, so a priestly allusion is at most secondary.

debates.bearing: John's explicit point is the fulfilment of Psalm 22. A priestly overtone fits the rest of his Gospel, where Jesus prays as an intercessor in John 17, but it should be held lightly and never made to carry the argument.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 2 gives the purpose of the whole wardrobe in two nouns, 'glory and splendor,' kavod and tiferet, and verse 40 repeats them for the sons. Kavod comes from a root meaning heavy or weighty, and it is the word for the glory of the LORD that fills the finished tabernacle, Exodus 40:34. Tiferet means beauty, splendour or adornment; Isaiah 52:1 calls Jerusalem to 'put on your garments of splendor.' The priest's clothes are not a neutral uniform. They are meant to carry weight and to be beautiful, reflecting in cloth and gold something of the One he serves.

The stones on the shoulders are 'memorial stones,' and the names on the breastpiece are a 'continual reminder before the LORD,' verses 12 and 29. Both translate zikkaron, from the verb zakar, to remember. When God 'remembered Noah,' Genesis 8:1, and 'remembered His covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob,' Exodus 2:24, remembering meant acting on behalf of those in view. Joshua 4:7 uses the same noun for stones that remind Israel. Here the reminder is placed 'before the LORD.' It is addressed to God, a standing appeal that He act for the twelve tribes whenever Aaron comes in.

The verb that runs through the chapter is nasa', to lift, carry or bear. Aaron bears names, verses 12 and 29, bears judgment, verse 30, and bears iniquity, verse 38. The phrase nasa' avon, to bear iniquity, has a wide range. It can mean to suffer the consequences of guilt, as in Leviticus 5:1, 'he shall bear the iniquity,' and in the warning of verse 43. It can mean to carry guilt away, as the scapegoat does, Leviticus 16:22. And with God as subject it means to forgive, Exodus 34:7. Isaiah 53:12 uses the verb for the Servant who 'bore the sin of many.' Verse 38 sits at the meeting point of those meanings.

The 'breastpiece of judgment' is choshen mishpat. Mishpat is justice, verdict or decision, and verse 30 says Aaron carries 'the judgment of the sons of Israel' over his heart. Numbers 27:21 speaks of seeking counsel 'by the judgment of the Urim.' The breastpiece carried both the people's names and God's decisions for them. The Greek Old Testament called it the logeion, the oracle, and rendered Urim and Thummim with words meaning disclosure and truth.

The gold 'plate' of verse 36 is tsits, a word that elsewhere means a blossom or flower, as in 'the flowers fall,' Isaiah 40:7. Exodus 29:6 and Leviticus 8:9 give it a second name, 'the holy diadem,' nezer. Nezer comes from the root for separation that also gives the word Nazirite, and Numbers 6:7 uses it for the Nazirite's 'crown of consecration.' The shining ornament on Aaron's brow is a crown of separation, setting him apart as belonging wholly to God.

typology.type: The names on Aaron's shoulders and over his heart, Exodus 28:12 and 28:29
typology.fulfillment: Aaron carried Israel on his shoulders, the place of strength, and over his heart, the place of affection and judgment, every time he went in. Christ carries His people in both ways. The shepherd who finds the lost sheep 'joyfully puts it on his shoulders,' Luke 15:5, and Jesus 'calls his own sheep by name,' John 10:3. He prays 'on behalf of those You have given Me,' John 17:9, and 'always lives to intercede for them,' Hebrews 7:25. The type falls short at two points: Aaron bore tribes, not persons, and he bore them only while he ministered. Christ knows each by name and never leaves the Father's presence.

typology.type: The gold plate, HOLY TO THE LORD, Exodus 28:36-38
typology.fulfillment: The plate made Aaron's holiness visible and allowed Israel's flawed gifts to be accepted. Yet the man who wore it could fashion a calf, Exodus 32:4; the holiness was engraved on gold rather than on his character. Christ is the high priest who is 'holy, innocent, undefiled, set apart from sinners,' Hebrews 7:26, and through Him spiritual sacrifices become 'acceptable to God,' 1 Peter 2:5. The escalation is that the inscription passes from the priest to the people: in the new Jerusalem God's name 'will be on their foreheads,' Revelation 22:4, for every servant, not for one man.

typology.type: The breastpiece of judgment carrying the Urim and Thummim, Exodus 28:30
typology.fulfillment: Through the priest Israel received God's decisions for the nation, Numbers 27:21, though the answers were limited and at times withheld, 1 Samuel 28:6. Hebrews opens by saying that God, who spoke in many ways, 'in these last days He has spoken to us by His Son,' Hebrews 1:2. In Christ the priest who represents the people and the word that reveals God's will are the same person. The type is a pattern of mediated guidance rather than a prediction, and it falls short because Christ does not answer with a yes or no drawn from a pouch but makes the Father known.

typology.type: Garments for glory and splendor, Exodus 28:2 and 28:40
typology.fulfillment: Aaron's dignity came from outside himself, from clothes God designed and Moses put on him, verse 41. John sees the risen Christ in 'a long robe, with a golden sash around His chest,' Revelation 1:13, glory that belongs to Him by nature and by His finished work. His people are then clothed from Him: all who were baptized into Christ 'have clothed yourselves with Christ,' Galatians 3:27, and the bride receives 'clothing of fine linen, bright and pure,' Revelation 19:8. Aaron's robes were handed down at death, Numbers 20:28; Christ's priesthood is permanent because He lives forever, Hebrews 7:24.

study.christ:
Hebrews builds its portrait of Jesus on the office this chapter creates. 'No one takes this honor upon himself; he must be called by God, just as Aaron was,' Hebrews 5:4, and Christ too was appointed by the Father, 5:5. Aaron was brought 'from among the Israelites,' verse 1, and every high priest is 'appointed from among men,' Hebrews 5:1. The Son became one of us for exactly this reason: He 'had to be made like His brothers in every way, so that He might become a merciful and faithful high priest,' Hebrews 2:17. The names over Aaron's heart find their meaning in a priest who is able 'to sympathize with our weaknesses,' Hebrews 4:15.

The two great works of the garments, bearing and interceding, are joined in Isaiah 53:12: 'He bore the sin of many and made intercession for the transgressors.' Aaron could carry names into the Holy Place and could wear a plate that covered the flaws of Israel's gifts. Christ carried sin itself: 'God made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf,' 2 Corinthians 5:21. And He has entered not a tent but 'heaven itself, now to appear on our behalf in the presence of God,' Hebrews 9:24. The phrase 'before the LORD' that echoes through Exodus 28 now describes where Jesus is.

The Gospels add a sobering contrast. At Jesus' trial the high priest, the man who wore these garments, 'tore his clothes,' Matthew 26:65, though Leviticus 21:10 forbade him to tear them. John records that this same Caiaphas, 'as high priest that year,' unknowingly prophesied that Jesus would die for the nation, John 11:51, a last flicker of the breastpiece's office of speaking God's judgment. Hours later the true high priest was stripped, and soldiers cast lots for His clothing, John 19:23-24. He came to His priestly work without glory or splendour, and the glory followed: the risen Christ appears in a long robe and golden sash, Revelation 1:13.

Some care is needed. The colours, the pomegranates and the individual gemstones are nowhere interpreted in the New Testament, and assigning each one a hidden meaning goes beyond the text. The link to Christ runs through the office the garments define, representation, remembrance, holiness, judgment and survival in God's presence, and through the New Testament's own use of the high priest. That is enough. When believers pray, they come as those whose names are already carried before the Father by a priest who will never take off His office.
study.god:
The chapter shows a God who wants to be remembered to, and who remembers. The stones are a 'memorial before the LORD,' verse 12, a 'continual reminder,' verse 29. God needs no prompting, yet He chooses to bind His attention to visible signs, just as He set the bow in the cloud so that He would 'remember' His covenant, Genesis 9:15. He stoops to a way of relating that His people can see and trust. When Aaron went in, Israel could know they were not forgotten.

He knows His people by name. Twelve names are cut twice, once on the shoulders in birth order, verse 10, and once on the breastpiece, verse 21. The last-born are carried as surely as the first. Reuben, who shamed his father, and Simeon and Levi, who shed blood at Shechem, are all there, Genesis 49:4-5. Inclusion rests on God's choosing, not on each tribe's record.

He is holy in a way that is dangerous to approach carelessly. Twice the chapter warns of death, 'so that he will not die,' verse 35, and 'so that they will not incur guilt and die,' verse 43. The bells announced the priest's movement in God's presence, and the linen undergarments preserved modesty at the altar, as Exodus 20:26 had already required. God is not casual about His own presence, and He will not be treated as though He were ordinary.

Yet the same God provides everything the danger requires. He designs the garments, fills the craftsmen with wisdom, verse 3, and gives Aaron a plate that makes Israel's imperfect gifts 'acceptable before the LORD,' verse 38. Holiness and grace are not rivals here. The holiness that could kill is the holiness that sets up the means of safe approach.

He is a God of beauty. He asks for 'glory and splendor,' verse 2, and for gold, fine linen, and gems cut with a jeweller's skill. Worship is not merely correct but lovely, because it reflects the One worshipped. He is also a God of judgment and guidance, placing the means of His decisions over the heart of the man who represents the people, verse 30.

For worship, this chapter moves in two directions at once. It humbles, because no one may walk into God's presence on their own terms. And it reassures, because God Himself has provided a priest who carries His people and whose holiness covers theirs.

crossReferences.note: The execution of this chapter's instructions, garment by garment, each section closing with 'just as the LORD had commanded Moses.' The repetition shows that nothing in the priest's dress was left to invention, and it confirms that the plan of chapter 28 was carried out exactly after the golden calf.

Moses dresses Aaron in the order of wearing rather than the order of description: tunic, sash, robe, ephod, breastpiece with the Urim and Thummim, turban and 'the gold plate, the holy diadem.' It is the moment chapter 28 was written for, and it shows that the priest is clothed by another.

On the Day of Atonement the high priest sets aside the gold and colour of Exodus 28 and enters the Most Holy Place in 'the sacred linen tunic, with linen undergarments.' The contrast shows that the garments of glory were not the garments of the deepest atonement, a humility that anticipates Christ.

Joshua is to stand before Eleazar, who 'will seek counsel for him before the LORD by the judgment of the Urim.' The verse shows the breastpiece of judgment in use, and it links Israel's leadership to the priest who carries God's decisions over his heart.

Joshua the high priest stands in filthy garments until God says, 'See, I have removed your iniquity,' and a clean turban is set on his head. It is Exodus 28 in reverse and then restored: the priest who should bear iniquity must first have his own removed by God.

The inscription of Exodus 28:36, once worn only on the high priest's forehead, is written 'on the bells of the horses,' and cooking pots become like altar bowls. The prophet looks to a day when the holiness concentrated on one man spreads through all of ordinary life.

Hebrews defines a high priest from the pattern of Aaron: taken from among men, dealing gently with the weak, called by God rather than self-appointed. Then it shows Christ fulfilling each condition, called by the Father who said, 'You are My Son.'

Because Jesus lives forever, His priesthood is permanent, and He 'always lives to intercede' for those who draw near. He is 'holy, innocent, undefiled,' the reality to which the gold plate on Aaron's turban could only point.

The risen Christ is seen 'dressed in a long robe, with a golden sash around His chest,' among the lampstands of His churches. The clothing is priestly as well as royal, and He is walking among His people as Aaron walked in the Holy Place.

The new Jerusalem has twelve gates 'inscribed with the names of the twelve tribes of Israel,' and verses 19 and 20 set precious stones in its foundations. The names and jewels once carried on one man's breast become the structure of the city where all God's people live.

In the new creation God's servants 'will see His face, and His name will be on their foreheads.' Aaron alone wore the Name's holiness on his brow in Exodus 28:38; at the end every servant bears it and stands in the presence Aaron entered with bells and fear.

Every Israelite was to wear a blue cord on the tassels of his garments so that he would remember God's commands and 'be holy to your God.' A thread of the priest's colour on ordinary clothing reminded the whole nation of its priestly calling in Exodus 19:6.

study.oneStory:
The story of clothing before God begins in Eden. The first pair were naked and unashamed, then sinned and tried to cover themselves, and God 'made garments of skin for Adam and his wife, and He clothed them,' Genesis 3:21. The word for those garments is the word for the tunics of Aaron's sons in verse 40. Exodus 28 takes up the same problem at a new stage: sinners cannot come before God uncovered, verse 42, and God Himself provides what they wear.

Eden echoes elsewhere too. Onyx was found in the land by the garden, Genesis 2:12, and it is the stone on Aaron's shoulders, verse 9. The man was placed in the garden 'to cultivate and keep it,' Genesis 2:15, and the Levites are later charged with the duties and service of the tabernacle in Numbers 3:7-8, where the Hebrew uses the same pair of verbs. The priest in the sanctuary is doing again, in a small way, what Adam was meant to do in God's garden.

God had called all Israel to be 'a kingdom of priests,' Exodus 19:6. Aaron stands in for that calling until it can be fulfilled, but the arrangement shows its limits almost at once. Aaron makes the calf, Exodus 32:4; two of his sons die at the altar, Leviticus 10:1-2; his robes pass to Eleazar at his death, Numbers 20:28. By the return from exile the Urim are gone, Ezra 2:63, and Zechariah sees the high priest in filthy clothes waiting for God to remove his iniquity, Zechariah 3:4.

The story turns in Christ. He is the priest who needed no clean turban, who carried sin rather than names, and who entered heaven itself. Through Him the priestly calling spreads to all His people, now 'a royal priesthood,' 1 Peter 2:9, and 'priests to His God and Father,' Revelation 1:6.

The new creation completes what Exodus 28 sketched. The city is a perfect cube, its length, width and height equal, Revelation 21:16, the shape of the inner sanctuary of Solomon's temple, 1 Kings 6:20. Its gates carry the names of the twelve tribes, its foundations are jewels, and every servant bears God's name on the forehead, Revelation 22:4. What was once engraved on one man's shoulders and heart becomes the dwelling of the whole people, and what was once written on one man's brow is written on all.

quiz.q: What was the stated purpose of Aaron's holy garments, according to verse 2?

options.text: To give him glory and splendor.
options.note: Verse 2 states this exact purpose for the garments.

options.text: To disguise him from the rest of Israel.
options.note: The garments were meant to display honor and holiness openly, not to conceal or disguise Aaron.

options.text: Purely for practical warmth in the wilderness.
options.note: No such practical purpose is mentioned; the stated reason is glory and splendor for his priestly office.

options.text: No purpose is given for the garments.
options.note: Verse 2 explicitly states the purpose: to give Aaron glory and splendor.

quiz.q: What was engraved on the two onyx stones mounted on the ephod's shoulder pieces?

options.text: The names of the sons of Israel, six on each stone.
options.note: Verses 9 through 10 describe this exact engraving.

options.text: The Ten Commandments in full.
options.note: The commandments were written on stone tablets kept in the ark, not engraved on the shoulder stones.

options.text: The name of Moses alone.
options.note: The stones bore the names of all twelve tribes, not a single individual's name.

options.text: The stones were left unengraved.
options.note: Verses 9 through 11 explicitly describe the engraving of Israel's tribal names.

quiz.q: What was placed inside the breastpiece of judgment, according to verse 30?

options.text: The Urim and Thummim.
options.note: Verse 30 specifies these were placed in the breastpiece over Aaron's heart.

options.text: A vial of anointing oil.
options.note: Anointing oil is described separately in chapter 30; the breastpiece specifically held the Urim and Thummim.

options.text: A copy of the covenant.
options.note: The covenant tablets, the Testimony, were placed in the ark, not the breastpiece.

options.text: The breastpiece was left empty.
options.note: Verse 30 explicitly commands the Urim and Thummim be placed within it.

quiz.q: Why did the robe of the ephod have gold bells and pomegranates around its hem?

options.text: So the sound would be heard when Aaron entered or exited the sanctuary, so that he would not die.
options.note: Verse 35 gives this exact, sober reason for the bells.

options.text: Purely for decorative musical effect during festivals.
options.note: The text gives a specific protective purpose tied to entering the sanctuary, not merely festive decoration.

options.text: To identify Aaron's rank compared to his sons.
options.note: The bells' stated purpose concerns entering the sanctuary safely, not signaling rank among priests.

options.text: No reason is given for the bells.
options.note: Verse 35 explicitly explains their purpose regarding entering and exiting the sanctuary.

quiz.q: What was inscribed on the gold plate worn on Aaron's forehead?

options.text: HOLY TO THE LORD.
options.note: Verse 36 gives this exact inscription.

options.text: The name of each tribe of Israel.
options.note: Tribal names were engraved on the shoulder stones and breastpiece gems, not on the forehead plate.

options.text: The Ten Commandments.
options.note: The commandments were written on the stone tablets in the ark, not on the forehead plate.

options.text: The plate bore no inscription.
options.note: Verse 36 explicitly gives the inscription: Holy to the LORD.

questions: Aaron carried Israel's names on his shoulders and over his heart every time he entered God's presence. How does it change your prayer life to know Christ carries your name before the Father in exactly that way, but perfectly?

The garments were made 'for glory and splendor,' yet their deepest purpose was to make Aaron's mediation possible at all. Where do you find yourself valuing the outward appearance of faith more than what it actually accomplishes before God?

The bells on Aaron's robe warned that carelessly entering God's presence could mean death. How does remembering the seriousness of approaching a holy God shape the reverence, or the casualness, of your own approach to Him?

The plate on Aaron's forehead let Israel's imperfect worship be counted holy before God. Where are you currently trying to make your own worship or service acceptable through effort, rather than resting in Christ's holiness on your behalf?

The Urim and Thummim gave Israel a way to seek God's judgment in specific matters. How do you currently seek God's guidance for decisions, and where might you need to trust Him more and control the outcome less?

translationNotes.note: The exact appearance and mechanism of the Urim and Thummim are not described anywhere in Scripture; they appear to have functioned as a means of discerning God's judgment, and their use had apparently ceased by the postexilic period, Ezra 2:63.

Bear the iniquity of the holy things describes Aaron's role in absorbing whatever ritual imperfection accompanied Israel's offerings, so that their gifts would still be accepted before the LORD, a striking anticipation of substitutionary mediation.

So that they will not incur guilt and die is repeated from verse 35 regarding the bells, underscoring that careless or improper approach to a holy God carried real, fatal consequences under the old covenant.
